newsitem.title: UK: Lebanon gets high speculative grade ratings.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon gets high speculative grade ratings.

text.p: Lebanon, hampered by worries about the country's fiscal and political backdrop, received high "speculative grade" credit ratings from international credit agencies on Wednesday.

The agencies, citing a strong banking system and economic progress, awarded Lebanon ratings at the top end of the speculative grade scale but they noted the scope for instability and the lack of a solid track record in public finances.
In Beirut, the acting Lebanese finance minister, Fouad Siniora, told Reuters that Moody's Investors Service had assigned Lebanon a B1 rating.

Standard & Poor's, which gave Lebanon a BB minus foreign currency long-term sovereign rating, separately said its ratings were constranied by Lebanese budget deficits averaging 14 percent of gross national product, a buildup of public debt and a vulnerable fiscal system.
But S&P said the situation could get better.

"Standard & Poor's base case scenario assumes that, despite occasional setbacks, geopolitical conditions will gradually improve. With Syria supporting the consensus on power sharing among Lebanon's confessional groups, Prime Minister Rafique Hariri should retain his dominant political position," it said.

"The 1998 presidential elections, a potential source of internal tension, should also proceed relatively smoothly. But Israel's occupation of south Lebanon, and relations between Israel and Syria, still pose obvious risks to Lebanon's reconstruction efforts, albeit ones consistent with current rating levels," S&P added.
The Lebanese government said the ratings received put it ahead of countries such as Brazil and Turkey, and on a par with countries such as Argentina and Jordan.

European rating agency IBCA gave Lebanon a BB long-term rating. It said Lebanon's rating was supported by a strong net external creditor position and by exceptional levels of liquid reserve assets at the central bank and in the banking system.
"These strengths offset concerns about the poor maturity structure of the external debt, and are also appropriate for a sovereign that faces unusual political vulnerabilities.

"Since the end of the civil war, the Lebanon has posted impressive growth rates and high levels of investment, both of which have been relatively resilient even in the face of shocks such as the April 1996 Israeli bombings," IBCA said.
Most importantly for the long term, IBCA said, the Lebanese private sector has real strengths, notably in the financial sector and in other services.

"The Lebanon, traditionally the banking and tourism centre for the region, is in a strong position to recapture its position given its traditions of liberal economic management, cultural freedom and entrepreneurial success," IBCA said.
